title: Algicidal Bacteria: A Review of Current Knowledge and Applications to Control Harmful Algal Blooms
authors: Coyne KJ, Wang Y, Johnson G
organism: Algicidal bacteria vs marine and freshwater HAB species
result: Reviews specificity, mechanisms and applications of algicidal bacteria and bacterial algicides. Notes that 'our understanding of these interactions is largely based on laboratory culture experiments', with only some field evidence.
env_effects: Review stresses that 'environmentally neutral' claims are untested; direct dispersal of live bacteria raises biosafety concerns, so immobilized or product-based deployment is proposed. Field evidence is limited to Pseudomonas fluorescens SK09 in river enclosures, with inconsistent results.
key_details: Narrative review of algicidal bacteria (specificity, algicidal compounds, mechanisms, application strategies). Its table of application studies is almost entirely laboratory work. The only field applications to date all used Pseudomonas fluorescens HYK0210-SK09 in river enclosures against the diatom Stephanodiscus hantzschii; strong lab and indoor-mesocosm effects gave inconsistent results in the field. Authors cite temperature, the high bacterial densities required, grazing by protists, pH and nutrients as reasons for field failure. No new quantitative data.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record is broadly right; it understates how thin the field evidence is (a single bacterial strain in river enclosures, with inconsistent results).

title: Algicidal Bacteria in the Sea and their Impact on Algal Blooms
organism: Marine algicidal bacteria vs eukaryotic microalgae
result: Concludes that, because of method limitations, 'the evidence for algicidal bacteria causing algal bloom decline is circumstantial'. Calls for ecosystem-level tests rather than a focus on HAB-control utility.
env_effects: Frames algicidy as part of bacterial regulation of algal community structure (i.e. community-wide, not target-only, effects).
key_details: Narrative review (Mayali & Azam) with sections on definition, taxonomy, mode of action, algicidal compounds, prey specificity and ecosystem considerations; no new data. Evidence that algicidal bacteria end blooms rests on MPN counts showing algicidal bacteria increase during bloom decline (e.g. Cytophaga during a Chattonella bloom), which the authors call 'no conclusive causal evidence'. In co-culture, algal lysis was seen only after the algicidal bacterium exceeded 10^6 cells/mL, about the abundance of the whole bacterial assemblage in seawater, raising doubt that a single species reaches that level in the ocean. Other bacteria in algal cultures can partly or fully block algicidal activity (e.g. against Karenia brevis). The authors suggest bloom decline may start from nutrient limitation, viruses or other pathogens, with algicidal bacteria as secondary colonizers.

title: Immobilization of algicidal bacterium Shewanella sp. IRI-160 and its application to control harmful dinoflagellates
organism: Shewanella sp. IRI-160 vs Karlodinium veneficum and Prorocentrum minimum; non-target Rhodomonas sp.
scale: Lab cultures; bacteria in agarose, alginate, sponge and foam matrices
dose: 10^6-10^8 bacterial cells/mL immobilized in alginate beads
result: Alginate retained >99% of Shewanella cells after 12 days, and bead-immobilized bacteria controlled K. veneficum and P. minimum as effectively as free bacteria. No harm to the non-target cryptophyte Rhodomonas.
env_effects: Containment in beads limits release of live bacteria; no effect on non-target Rhodomonas.

title: Bacteria-Produced Algicide for Field Control of Toxic Dinoflagellates Does Not Cause a Cortisol Stress Response in Two Estuarine Fish Species
authors: Simons VE, Targett TE, Gaffney PM, Coyne KJ
organism: Algicide IRI-160AA (from Shewanella IRI-160); non-target fish Fundulus heteroclitus and Menidia menidia
scale: Five ~400 L recirculating systems, each with ten ~20 L tanks (one fish per tank), 25 ppt seawater
dose: IRI-160AA at 1% v/v (EC50 for Karlodinium veneficum)
duration: Laboratory exposures with diel-cycling hypoxia and/or pH at 25 and 30 °C
result: Exposure to IRI-160AA did not significantly change plasma cortisol in either fish species at either temperature, alone or combined with hypoxia/pH cycling. Non-target safety study, no algal endpoint.
env_effects: No neuroendocrine stress response in two estuarine fish (Long Island Sound species) at the algicidal dose.

title: Evaluation of a virus-based control method to protect cultured oysters from the harmful dinoflagellate Heterocapsa circularisquama
authors: Nakayama N, Hamaguchi M, Yamaguchi H, Masuda K, Fujiwara M
organism: RNA virus HcRNAV vs Heterocapsa circularisquama
scale: One treatment and one control 15,000 L floating 'cage' mesocosm in Lake Kamo (saltwater lake connected to the sea), Sado Island, Japan, plus lab tests; n = 3 refers to replicate samples, not replicate mesocosms
dose: 1.4 kg of local surface sediment containing HcRNAV (frozen at -20 °C for one day) sprayed into 15,000 L, i.e. ~0.093-0.1 g sediment/L, at a bloom density of ~3800 cells/mL (October 2016)
result: H. circularisquama in the sediment-treated mesocosm fell to ~1% of the initial density after five days, while the untreated control also fell, to 20-30%; the treatment was significantly lower than control from day 3 onward (GLM, p < .01), and HcRNAV in water rose significantly by day 2.
env_effects: Sediment addition (0.093 g/L) judged negligible for bacteria, nutrients and turbidity; temperature, salinity and nutrients did not differ between treatment and control. Unpublished tests: sediment (1-10 g/L) and HcRNAV did not affect survival of juvenile oysters, pearl oysters or clams, and HcRNAV strains did not infect Karenia mikimotoi, Chattonella or Heterosigma strains. Freezing inactivated cysts in the sediment so no other HAB species emerged.
key_details: Paired floating mesocosms (one treatment, one control, 15,000 L each) during a natural H. circularisquama bloom (~3800 cells/mL) in Lake Kamo, October 2016, plus lab dose tests. Treatment received 1.4 kg of HcRNAV-bearing lake sediment (~0.1 g/L). Density fell to ~1% of initial after five days versus 20-30% in the untreated control, so much of the decline also happened without treatment; treatment-control difference significant from day 3 (GLM, p < .01). The design has no mesocosm replication (one of each), and the bloom was already declining in the control. Environmental safety claims rest partly on unpublished results.
fulltext_discrepancy: The record's 'n = 3' implies replicated mesocosms; there was one treatment and one control mesocosm (n = 3 was sample replication). The record omits that the control bloom also dropped to 20-30% of initial in five days, so the ~99% headline overstates the treatment effect relative to control. The site is a saltwater lake (Lake Kamo), not an oyster farm as such.

title: Viral Impacts on Total Abundance and Clonal Composition of the Harmful Bloom-Forming Phytoplankton Heterosigma akashiwo
authors: Tarutani K, Nagasaki K, Yamaguchi M
organism: HaV (Heterosigma akashiwo virus) vs Heterosigma akashiwo
scale: Field time series at surface and bottom in northern Hiroshima Bay (May-July 1998) plus cross-infection tests of H. akashiwo isolates against co-occurring HaV clones
result: H. akashiwo reached 6.5 x 10^3 to 1.4 x 10^5 cells/mL (up to 90% of phytoplankton) and crashed as HaV rose, but persisted at 10^1-10^2 cells/mL; mean susceptibility of isolates fell from 59% (bloom) to 18% (post-bloom) of HaV clones, then recovered to 61% as resistant cells were displaced.
env_effects: Host resistance emerges after viral termination, limiting repeated use of one virus strain.
key_details: Observational field study of a natural bloom, not a control treatment; no virus was added and there is no untreated control. Host isolates from three periods were each challenged with the co-occurring HaV clones (lysis checked for 10-14 days). Isolate susceptibility during the post-bloom period II (18% +/- 23%) was significantly lower than in periods I and III (59% +/- 40%, 61% +/- 37%; Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.001). The bloom collapse coincided with HaV increase, but a resistant residual population of 10^1-10^2 cells/mL survived. Causation of the crash by virus is inferred from correlation.
fulltext_discrepancy: None material; record lacked the densities and the susceptibility percentages, and should note that virus causation is correlational (no manipulation).

title: Resistance of the fish-killing dinoflagellate Cochlodinium polykrikoides against algicidal bacteria isolated from the coastal sea of Japan
organism: Six algicidal bacteria vs Cochlodinium (Margalefidinium) polykrikoides
dose: Six bacterial isolates from Japanese coastal waters
result: Per Semantic Scholar summary, C. polykrikoides was resistant to all six algicidal bacteria tested, possibly reflecting mixotrophy, which may help prolong its red tides. No quantitative data seen.

title: A Novel Jumbo Phage PhiMa05 Inhibits Harmful Microcystis sp.
authors: Naknaen A, Suttinun O, Surachat K, Khan E, Pomwised R
scale: Lab cultures (96-well plates, 20 mL cultures; planktonic and aggregated cells)
duration: Up to 14 days; total lysis in 3-4 days at high MOI
result: Lytic phage with burst size ~127 and 1-day latent period; host cultures collapsed within 3 days at MOI 100 and after 3-4 days at MOI 10 and 1. Lysis significantly reduced total microcystins vs uninfected cultures.
env_effects: No lysogeny, toxin or antibiotic-resistance genes found in the genome; lysis releases intracellular microcystins into water.

title: A Review of Cyanophage–Host Relationships: Highlighting Cyanophages as a Potential Cyanobacteria Control Strategy
authors: Grasso CR, Pokrzywinski KL, Waechter C, Rycroft T, Zhang Y, Aligata A, Kramer M, Lamsal A
organism: Cyanophages vs Synechococcus, Microcystis, Dolichospermum, Aphanizomenon, Cylindrospermopsis, Planktothrix, Lyngbya
result: Reviews cyanophage life cycles, diversity and infectivity for seven North American cyanoHAB genera and discusses efficacy, optimization and scalability. Highlights high specificity and self-propagation as advantages.
env_effects: High host specificity (many phages infect only one strain), so mixed blooms and resistant strains limit control; dosing is not standardized (many studies add an undefined 'cyanophage concentrate' at 10% v/v); propagation in the field depends on nutrients, light and temperature and is untested.
key_details: Literature review of cyanophage biology and cyanophage-host relationships for seven cyanoHAB genera; no new experiments. It reports no field or mesocosm cyanophage control trials; the evidence base is lab infection assays. Authors note that 'cyanophage concentrate' added at 10% v/v has become an accepted but imprecise dosing standard and call for standardized dose-response work before field use. Examples: Ma-LMM01 infects only one M. aeruginosa strain; PaV-LD from Lake Donghu infected only P. agardhii isolates from the same lake.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record implies minimal non-target impacts as an advantage; the full text frames extreme specificity and lack of dosing standards as major barriers, with no field evidence at all.

title: Facilitating harmful algae removal in fresh water via joint effects of multi-species algicidal bacteria
authors: He L, Lin Z, Wang Y, He X, Zhou J, Guan M, Zhou J
organism: Enriched multi-species algicidal bacteria (Bacillus, Pseudomonas, etc.) vs natural freshwater phytoplankton
result: Under optimal conditions the algicidal ratio reached 87.69% with Chl a degradation of 47.00 µg/(L·d). Bacteria and filler light shading accounted for 53.74% and 36.47% of inhibition, respectively.
env_effects: Released dissolved organic matter and disinfection by-product precursors (fluorescence, UV254) were assessed.

title: The potential of prodigiosin for control of Prorocentrum donghaiense blooms: Algicidal properties and acute toxicity to other marine organisms at various trophic levels
authors: Chen Y, Luo G, Chen S, Zhang D, Xie W, Wang Z, Zheng W, Xu H
organism: Bacterial pigment prodigiosin vs Prorocentrum donghaiense; non-targets Chlorella vulgaris, Photobacterium phosphoreum, Artemia salina, Lateolabrax japonicus
scale: Lab cultures and acute toxicity tests
dose: Prodigiosin (from Zooshikella sp. SZ14) 0.01-0.2 ug/mL; 0.05 ug/mL = inhibitory dose, 0.1 ug/mL = algicidal dose
duration: 12-72 h algicidal assays; 96 h fish test
result: Prodigiosin 24 h LC50 was 0.046 ug/mL for P. donghaiense; >=0.08 ug/mL killed 97% of cells by 48 h with no recovery by 72 h, while 0.03-0.05 ug/mL cells recovered to initial density by 72 h. The 0.1 ug/mL control dose was toxic to Artemia (24 h LC50 0.123 ug/mL) and sea bass juveniles (24 h LC50 0.125 ug/mL; 19.6% killed at 0.1 ug/mL in 24 h).
env_effects: At the algicidal dose (0.1 ug/mL) prodigiosin killed 49.3% of Artemia salina nauplii in 24 h and 19.6% of Lateolabrax japonicus juveniles in 24 h; fish 96 h NOEC 0.05 ug/mL. Chlorella vulgaris unaffected up to 1 ug/mL (24 h LC50 31.8 ug/mL); Photobacterium growth slowed to ~74-76% of control at 0.05-0.1 ug/mL.
key_details: Lab flask assays, at least triplicate, with cell counts every 12 h after prodigiosin dosing of P. donghaiense cultures. 0.03 and 0.05 ug/mL killed 29% and 53% of cells at 24 h, but survivors regrew to initial density by 72 h (attributed to photodegradation); 0.08-0.2 ug/mL gave >80% kill at 24 h and 97% at 48 h. Fv/Fm fell 20.6% and 93.4% below control after 3 h at 0.05 and 0.1 ug/mL. Non-target tests: Artemia 24/48 h LC50 0.123/0.088 ug/mL, sea bass juveniles 24/48 h LC50 0.125/0.116 ug/mL, Chlorella 24 h LC50 31.8 ug/mL, Photobacterium 15 min EC50 0.505 ug/mL. The safety margin between the algicidal dose and animal LC50s is only about 1.2x.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record implies non-targets are safe ('less sensitive than the HAB'); in fact the 0.1 ug/mL algicidal dose killed 49.3% of Artemia nauplii and 19.6% of juvenile sea bass within 24 h, and LC50s for both are only ~1.2x the control dose. Dose was missing from the record.

title: The Algicidal Fungus Trametes versicolor F21a Eliminating Blue Algae via Genes Encoding Degradation Enzymes and Metabolic Pathways Revealed by Transcriptomic Analysis
authors: Dai W, Chen X, Wang X, Xu Z, Gao X, Jiang C, Deng R, Han G
organism: White-rot fungus Trametes versicolor F21a vs Microcystis aeruginosa PCC7806
dose: Fungal mycelia pre-grown 5 days (from a 7 mm plug in 15 mL potato medium) transferred into 100 mL of algal culture
result: About 85% of M. aeruginosa cells were eliminated within 30 h and chlorophyll-a fell to one sixth of the initial content; fungal DEGs rose from 193 to 742 over 0-30 h. Commercial decomposition enzymes alone only partially inhibited algal growth.
key_details: Lab co-culture of T. versicolor F21a mycelia with M. aeruginosa PCC7806 in 250 mL flasks (25 C, 90 umol photons m-2 s-1, 120 rpm). Chl-a declined gradually over the first 12 h to one sixth of initial after 30 h; about 85% of algal cells eliminated; fungal biomass rose about 12% (p < 0.05). RNA-Seq with two biological replicates per time point; qPCR validation with three. Main purpose is transcriptomic mechanism, not control efficacy; a single lab strain at flask scale with no environmental tests.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record said the target was generic 'blue algae' and gave no efficacy number; full text gives M. aeruginosa PCC7806 and 85% cell removal in 30 h.
